introduction.title: Introduction Log
introduction.body:
Welcome to my blog! Here, I'll share my absurd and random research about various topics that interest me. You should expect Neurology, logic, Math, Programming, and a few more related matters. I'm starting this blog becuase I want to learn more about React and programming as a whole. Although, to be honest, one of the main reasons is that I admire my brother more than I let on, and he has a blog, so I'm kind of copying his idea too... Either way, I'm really excited for the future this can have.

About myself, there is one thing I think describes me very accrurately; I love to think. I spend hours looking out the window and thinking, or imagining, or anything related to the use of my brain. I believe the human brain is the greatest invention of nature, though you could argue that it is the one saying that, so it has no value.
Enough Neurology, I also think that I'm accrurately described by my annoying need to be grammatically and spellingly correct, which I hope I achieved in this few paragraphs. Lastly, my like for Maths and Programming probably describe a lot about me too, like the fact that I enjoy rule-based or logic stuff.

This log was more of a casual introduction, most logs will be actual research with facts and ideas. Well, that is it for this log, bye whoever is reading this (if anyone)!

information_for_choice.title: Information for Choice
information_for_choice.body:
I was just discussing an important choice I have to make with my brother, and despite his "brother mocking" (yeah, that's what I'm calling it), I think I actually learned from that interaction.

Making decisions is something we do every second, like choosing to read this right now or scratching my arm while I think about how to continue this sentence. The frontal lobe plays an important role in decision-making, while the hippocampus helps us use past experiences to imagine and evaluate future possibilities.

Dopamine also affects the choices we make, but not quite in the way people often describe it. It is involved in motivation and learning from rewards: when an outcome is better or worse than we expected, dopamine signals can help us update what we are likely to choose in the future. The amygdala contributes by helping us process the emotional significance of an outcome, rather than by producing dopamine or hormones itself. Thus, positive or negative experiences can influence the decisions we make later on. That said, I will now add my own ideas, which are not related to neuroscience.

Deciding on something requires options to choose from; otherwise, we would be imagining rather than deciding. I also think we need some idea of what those options are. If you have three choices but do not fully understand them, then the ones you do not understand are not really choices yet, only small representations of them. This creates a problem when choosing what to learn: you have to choose among things you do not yet know, which is exactly why you want to learn them. I think this can be explained by saying that, at that point, every option is only a representation, so the choices are equally valid. Now that I have established my idea of choice, I can talk about the process of choosing.

If we liked all options equally, choosing would be impossible. We could still decide by chance, such as by spinning a wheel or flipping a coin, but that would not tell us which option is better. In reality, I think there is often a better choice, though identifying it is much harder. Say you are choosing a job and listing the pros and cons of each one. How do you know you are not favouring one by noticing more of its advantages? You might list that one job pays well, but forget to list that another is close to home. It is hard to consider every good and bad quality of two options with equal attention.

Then how can we compare them? You could start one job and, after a year, decide whether to stay or switch. But that has two problems. First, you may have spent a year of your limited life in a job that was less rewarding than the other. Second, you may decide to stay and miss out on the job that might have been more rewarding. To know how rewarding each job is before trying it, you would have to experience it; but if you have not experienced it, you cannot rate it properly, and if you cannot rate it, how can you choose? We loop all the way back.

This is the paradox of choosing without a cost. Maybe the best solution is to spend one year in each job. At first, that seems better, but it also removes the possibility of an unbiased comparison. You might prefer one because of the stage of life in which you did it, or because it came first and now feels nostalgic. Either way, your experience has changed you, so comparing the two jobs fairly becomes difficult. You could say that you should choose the one you prefer now, because it gives you the greater reward immediately, but perhaps the other would be better in the long run.

I have finished explaining my problems with making a decision, and now I have to reach a conclusion. Sadly, I have not solved this problem for myself either, and although I have over two months, I do not think I will be able to choose correctly. My brother suggests one option, and I admire him greatly, so it would be reasonable to follow his advice. But I am very different from him, so who is to say I will like what he liked? On the other hand, a man similar to my brother, who made the opposite choice, told me that I will probably prefer what he (this man) chose. This is the big paradox of choosing: one that, even after years of thinking, I do not think I will ever fully escape. Thanks for reading.
